items.title: U.S. sues Lyft, alleges it denied rides to passengers with service dogs and wheelchairs
items.description: The US Justice Department sued Lyft LYFT.O on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing ​services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs.

items._ogDesc: The US Justice Department sued Lyft LYFT.O on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing ​services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs.
items.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 9 - The U.S. Justice Department sued Lyft LYFT.O on Monday, alleging the ride-hailing ​services provider discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs.

The lawsuit seeks US$53 million for individuals with disabilities who Lyft allegedly discriminated against, and who have submitted complaints to Lyft or the Department of Justice, the DOJ said in a statement.

Lyft did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit, which was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

The lawsuit alleges Lyft violated Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which prohibits private transportation companies from discriminating based on disability.

The lawsuit seeks a court order to force Lyft to stop the alleged discrimination, to modify its policies to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, and to train its staff and drivers on the law, the Justice Department said.

The Justice Department alleged that Lyft and its drivers routinely refuse service to individuals with disabilities and refuse to reasonably modify Lyft’s policies and practices to avoid such discrimination.

Last year, the US government sued Uber UBER.N, accusing the ride-sharing company of violating the same federal law by discriminating against passengers with disabilities.

That lawsuit sought $125 million for individuals subjected to the alleged discrimination and who previously submitted complaints to Uber or the Justice Department.

Uber had said it disagreed with all of the allegations, and was committed to expanding access and improving the experience of riders with disabilities.

Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Caitlin Webber, Reuters

items.title: Canada launches instant payments network after years of delay
items.description: Payments Canada says it has launched its real-time rail national payment system, which is expected to speed day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Bay Street Financial District is shown in Toronto on Friday, August 5, 2022. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nathan Denette]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Nathan Denette</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Payments Canada says it has launched its real-time rail national payment system, which is expected to speed day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Payments Canada says it has launched its real-time rail national payment system, which is expected to speed day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers.

It says the new system is expected to enable participating members to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time.

“The launch of Canada’s real-time rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” Payments Canada CEO Susan Hawkins said in a news release Monday.

“As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the (real-time rail) gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on.”

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The system is expected to generate savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques and a shorter period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient.

The initial participants include Wealthsimple, Questbank, Peoples Trust Co., Paramount Commerce, Koho, DoBusiness.com, Digital Commerce Bank and Bank of America. Additional participants are expected to be added in the coming months, including all of the major Canadian financial institutions.

Transactions that pass through Payments Canada systems include debit card payments, pre-authorized debits, direct deposits, bill payments, wire payments and cheques.

Henry Kim, a professor at York University’s Schulich School of Business, said the announcement is a step in the right direction.

“There’s a thread that we have to do this for our sovereignty, and we just have to keep up with the rest of the world. A lot of the world has real-time settlement,” he said in an interview, adding it already exists in the U.S.

Payments Canada has been years behind schedule on getting the system in place, which allows near-instant payments clearing 24 hours a day, along with other improvements. The organization originally aimed to have the system in place by 2019.

The ability to more rapidly clear payments is particularly helpful for businesses, Kim said.

“It also means that if you’re tight for cash, if you’re a business and your working capital runs low, you can get paid much faster by other businesses,” he said.

Payments Canada said the real-time rail system will also come with mandatory centralized fraud services and controls, including confirmation of payee, a fraud transaction safety score, a list of fraud risks, and a platform for fraud reporting.

Kim, who works with U.S. credit unions on payment technology, said there are some concerns among U.S. financial institutions about fraud-related risks from real-time payments, with some U.S. banks electing not to provide the feature to customers.

“Because when you get rid of that lag, there’s less time for verification so someone could actually make a fraudulent transaction. And with the real-time rail, oftentimes you don’t get that back,” he said.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

“Canada’s actually done something different from the U.S., and I think it’s actually really good to have that centralized.”

Claire Célérier, Canada Research Chair in household finance and an associate professor at the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management, said that even though Canada is playing catch-up to other countries, there are advantages to not being the first mover.

“When you develop such an infrastructure, reliability is absolutely crucial. There are strong concerns regarding fraud and I think what Canada has been able to develop is potentially an infrastructure that is more robust to fraud,” she said.

The question now, she said, is what fees retail banking customers may face for faster transfers.

“It should decrease the fees of payment transfer by a lot, but I hope it will be the case and that it will be monitored to make sure that everyone can benefit from this instant payment at a low cost,” she said.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

items.title: U.S. Senate to take first major action since midterm elections
items.description: The U.S. Senate is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centres and other infrastructure projects.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Capitol is seen under a gray autumn sky in Washington, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">J. Scott Applewhite</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The U.S. Senate is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centres and other infrastructure projects.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centres and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now faces yearslong delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centres pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centres and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

Midterm results could complicate bill’s passage in lame-duck session

While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats’ sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centres powered by natural gas.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.

The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

“Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly US$4 billion on such settlements.

Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.

Trump told reporters Monday that he still opposes wind energy. When told that wind is part of the bill, Trump replied: “Well, the bill hasn’t been fully negotiated. I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland voted against moving the legislation forward, in part due to Trump’s opposition to offshore wind. Van Hollen said the bill does not fully address the administration’s efforts to block Maryland’s pending offshore wind project, which he said would lower energy costs for households across the state and create thousands of jobs.

Senate sponsors are optimistic the bill will pass both chambers

At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” next year.

White House said Trump’s support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.

Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.

Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centres instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, he said.

Capito called the bill “a win for America,’’ adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity ... to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

Industry leaders are advocating for the bill’s passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.

While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.

Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.

“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk,” she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

Matthew Daly And Jennifer McDermott, The Associated Press

McDermott reported from Providence, R.I.

items.title: Culture minister insists Canada will eventually force streaming giants to pay fair share for CanCon
items.description: Canada's identity and culture minister insists the federal government will force streaming giants to pay their fair share to contribute to Canadian content, but wouldn’t say when that will happen.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Canadian Identity and Culture Minister Marc Miller attend a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday, June 10, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canada's identity and culture minister insists the federal government will force streaming giants to pay their fair share to contribute to Canadian content, but wouldn’t say when that will happen.
items.body:
OTTAWA – Canadian Identity and Culture Minister Marc Miller insists the federal government will force streaming giants to pay their fair share to contribute to Canadian content, though he wouldn’t answer when pressed on when that will happen.

The federal government’s latest budget, tabled in the House of Commons last week, earmarks money to amplify Canadian “cultural sovereignty,” including $600 million to support domestic news and cultural content.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Miller, in an interview on CTV Power Play with Vassy Kapelos on Monday, said the funds are being “deployed on a relatively emergency basis,” to ensure support for the industry.

A background document for the announcement stipulates the funds will help sustain Canadian content creation and mitigate the impact of declining private-sector contributions from cable and satellite companies, as well as expected contributions from international streaming platforms.

In June, meanwhile, the federal government directed the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commissions (CRTC) to review its recent decision to triple the amount it charges digital streaming companies to contribute to Canadian content.

Digital streaming giants — including American companies such as Netflix and Disney — were previously required to contribute five per cent of their Canadian revenues to domestic content.

In late May, the CRTC announced its decision to triple the amount from five to 15 per cent.

The federal government has yet to collect any of those funds, however, with a number of streaming companies fighting the decision in court.

Speaking to Kapelos, Miller insisted the $600-million injection into Canadian content is not bowing down to outside pressure, in particular from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration, which has frequently cited the Online Streaming Act as a trade irritant.

He said while Canada’s legislation to support Canadian content have been “noble,” it hasn’t worked to “(make) sure that money is being redistributed into the system in the face of dwindling ad revenue from different sources.”

Miller was part of the previous Liberal government, which passed its legislative framework for regulating streamers, the Online Streaming Act, in April 2023.

The minister categorized the funding announced in the budget as “a practical short-term approach.”

“We need to take that next step to make sure that the large streamers that are here — that sometimes do very important work in terms of supporting Canadian content — are actually contributing to our ecosystem, because they’re getting money from streamers,” Miller said.

“This is not an uncomplex discussion, but it is one that, as part of the budget announcement, is only partial in how we have moved to support through cash and through financial support,” he added. “Whereas we have a next step of the puzzle that is yet to be completed in making sure that the CRTC is making sure that these large streamers are contributing to the ecosystem.”

The minister said it’s “a question of fairness” that large streamers pay more for domestic content when they are benefitting from Canadian viewers, but taking the profit out of the country.

Asked by Kapelos about a timeline to figure out how much the CRTC will collect from streamers, Miller wouldn’t directly answer, saying only that his department wants to get the directives out “as quickly as possible”.

And, when pressed on the fact it’s already been more than five months since the federal government asked the CRTC to reconsider the amount it charges streamers, Miller said he’ll take his time to issue a directive “that makes sense.”

He said the last time the government asked the CRTC to come up with regulations for the Online Streaming Act, it took three years, so he’s hoping it’s faster this time around.

Miller said the point of the legislation is to encourage big companies to be “good corporate citizens,” and to that end he is now considering changing the tax system for streamers.

“We also support those companies in terms of very generous tax credits that allow them to do business in a profitable fashion in Canada,” Miller told Kapeos. “I want to take another look at how that is being done and how these companies are benefiting from a tax system that they are seeking to remove revenue from.”

You can watch Canadian Identity and Culture Minister Marc Miller’s full interview on CTV Power Play with Vassy Kapelos in the video player at the top of this article.

items.title: Canada Post says higher international and U.S. mail costs will sustain its operations
items.description: A Canada Post spokesperson says the planned increase in the price of stamps is meant to help the Crown corporation become self-sustaining after years of financial losses.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Canada Post mailbox is pictured in Richmond B.C. on Friday, Sept. 26, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Ethan Cairns]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">ETHAN CAIRNS</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A Canada Post spokesperson says the planned increase in the price of stamps is meant to help the Crown corporation become self-sustaining after years of financial losses.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The planned increase in the price of stamps is meant to help Canada Post become self-sustaining after years of financial losses, the Crown corporation’s chief spokesperson said.

Last week’s federal budget announced the price of a single domestic stamp will go from $1.44 to $2 in 2027, with a seven per cent increase in cost each year after.

Jon Hamilton, Canada Post’s vice-president of communications, said this move is an attempt to better match the prices consumers pay with the organization’s operating costs and help repay some of the assistance Ottawa has provided to keep Canada Post afloat.

“We are just trying to return to the price of the service aligning more with the cost of providing the service, because it’s been out of whack for a number of years,” he said.

He said the price for U.S.-bound and international letter stamps will also go up but the amount has not yet been decided.

Canada Post is not changing the price of parcel shipping, which it says is a market-driven product.

Tara Joy Andrews of Enchanted Postmark Snail Mail Club said the price increase will affect how many Canadians use the mail.

“There is already a reduced number of people sending mail, and this increase will make that even smaller. Although snail mail and sending letters and postcards to pen pals are growing in popularity, I feel this increase will reduce how much people send,” Joy Andrews said in an email.

Her club provides subscribers with monthly postcards and stationery, with the goal of members sending letters of their own with the materials. The aim is to brighten someone’s day with the “simple joy of receiving mail.”

In February, the federal government gave Canada Post $1.01 billion in the form of a repayable loan to help the organization maintain services.

The recent budget proposes another $1.4 billion over two years to help support the Crown corporation’s operations.

It would also provide $1.2 billion over seven years to support Canada Post’s move to community mailboxes.

Hamilton said most Canadian mailboxes have been centralized already.

“Of the roughly 18 million addresses across the country, there’s only about four million left that still get door-to-door delivery. As we move forward we’re going to be converting those four million addresses,” he said.

Canada Post’s annual report says the Crown corporation saw $1.57 billion in pre-tax losses in 2025, the highest amount on record.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026

Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

items.title: Nvidia CEO admits to affair with woman suspected of being spy for China
items.description: China denied on Monday there was a spy plot attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, calling the spying allegations unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[This image taken from video in 2024 shows Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (right), with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang (left). (Reuters)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: China denied on Monday there was a spy plot attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, calling the spying allegations unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.
items.body:
BANGKOK — China denied on Monday there was a spy plot attempt to ensnare Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, calling the spying allegations unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Huang has acknowledged to the Nvidia board that he had been intimate with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing, according to The New York Times.

“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday.

Also on Monday, Nvidia shares dropped roughly five per cent in pre-market trading.

The chips company CEO is at the centre of a controversy over whether he drove sales of advanced computer chips to China, in spite of U.S. tech restrictions aimed at limiting China’s ability to access these advanced technologies. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft.

Nvidia said on Sunday that the company would launch an investigation into the case. Huang did not name the person in the extramarital affair.

China had previously denied the New York Times report that said Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that faced claims of smuggling advanced chips into China, and that she was a spy for Beijing.

“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

“Those questions require evidence rather than speculation,” he added in a text message to reporters.

Huang had pushed to loosen chip sales restrictions to China in recent years, successfully lobbying U.S. President Donald Trump to allow his company to sell H200 chips this year. However, it is uncertain if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy these chips en masse. Nvidia said in a filing in August that it sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.

While those chips are not Nvidia’s most cutting-edge models, they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to sell the less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed for the Chinese market while complying with U.S. export restrictions.

Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations.

“Whenever China-U.S. relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows,” the state-owned Global Times said.

Associated Press business writer Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong contributed to this report.

Huizhong Wu, The Associated Press

items.title: ‘Betrayed our members’ Unifor President reacts to Stellantis sale of Brampton assembly plant
items.description: Stellantis has announced the sale of its Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defence technology company Roshel.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The Stellantis vehicle assembly plant and Unifor National President Lana Payne in a combination photo. (THE CANADIAN PRESS/Nathan Denette/CTV News)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Stellantis has announced the sale of its Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defence technology company Roshel.
items.body:
Stellantis has announced the sale of its Brampton assembly plant to Canadian defence technology company Roshel, a move that a union representing workers says amounts to a “betrayal.”

In a news release issued late Monday afternoon, Stellantis and Roshel announced an agreement to sell the plant “for an undisclosed amount,” with the transaction expected to close by the end of this year.

The sale, they said, will “create a path to return the Brampton Assembly Plant to productive industrial use.”

More than 2,200 workers have been on layoff at the Brampton assembly plant since production was put on hold in December, 2023.

“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said in the release.

“With this announcement, we are driving forward our broader strategic goals, opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”

‘Stellantis has betrayed our members’

In a press conference Monday evening, Unifor President Lana Payne, said that the sale of the plant “has been and will be an unacceptable outcome for our union and our members.”

“Selling an auto assembly plant and losing vehicle production capacity is devastating for the Canadian industry, for our country, but mostly for the workers who have given so much to this company over so many years. Because once that capacity is gone, it’s often gone for good,” Payne said.

Payne described the sale as a “worst case scenario” and that Stellantis “has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers.”

Payne called the sale a “continued breach” of the company’s commitments and said that “allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of our national auto strategy, and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect auto workers from this U.S. trade war.”

“It’s really hard to believe this plant could have been sold without some green light from the federal government, Payne said.”

Later in the press conference, Unifor Local President Vito Biato also condemmed the sale, and said that they told government officials that the move would “steer the auto industry down the wrong path.”

“Some in government are hearing us, but just aren’t listening.”

“Workers have done nothing but build the best cars for this company for decades. These same workers are now left chasing rumours. Stellantis has disrespected our members and our union. This is complete shameful and disgusting behaviour by Stellantis,” Biato said.

Unifor officials said they had requested a meeting with Stellantis and government officials about the Brampton plant sale.

In a statement, the union asked the City of Brampton and the Ontario government to “take all possible actions” to enforce bylaws which “explicitly designate the Brampton Assembly Plant location for automotive assembly.”

Deal ends months of speculation

In September, Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel for a potential sale of the plant, setting off months of speculation on its fate.

On Monday, Roshel said that it plans to “create a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing” which will “allow Canadian companies to better serve customers at home and export into allied markets.”

Roshel did not provide details on how many people would be employed at the facility, only saying that once complete it will “bring much-needed manufacturing space and jobs to the Toronto area.”

In an interview with CTV News, Roshel CEO Roman Shimonoz said that his company plans to “maintain its purpose and to continue employing people under the automotive activity.”

“We are looking and exploring different ways to ensure that we can create 1000s of jobs, and we’re doing that without waiting. And it’s very easy to criticise and be negative, but what is the alternative? This plant was idle for over three years. We now have a much better future, not just for people of this plant, but for Brampton, for Ontario, for Canada.”

Stellantis received funding to retool plant

In May, 2022 the federal government agreed to provide Stellantis with $529 million in funding to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants.

In a statement, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the decision by Stellantis “does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton.”

“We remain focused on finding solutions for the more than 2,000 affected workers and their families. They deserve answers, respect and, above all, a secure future,” Joly wrote. “All parties must come back to the bargaining table. I have reached out to representatives from Unifor, Stellantis, the Government of Ontario and the Brampton plant to convene a meeting later this week.”

There is a long history of manufacturing at the Brampton assembly plant dating back to 1986.

Most recently, the Dodge Charger and Dodge Challenger were assembled at the plant but the last of those vehicles rolled off the assembly line in 2023.

At the time, Stellantis said that the plant would undergo improvements to begin manufacturing electric vehicles.

In a statement, Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown reacted to the news saying that “the members of Unifor Local 1285 and their families have lived with years of uncertainty. They deserve a fair resolution from Stellantis and a clear path to good-paying jobs.”

“I’m calling on Stellantis to work with Unifor to reach that resolution, and on Roshel to work directly with Local 1285 to identify hiring and training opportunities for laid-off Brampton autoworkers,” Brown said.

“Stellantis must repay taxpayers for the public funding it received to support automotive production in Brampton. I will continue pressing the federal government to recover that money and hold Stellantis accountable for the commitments it made to our workers and our city.”

Opposition leaders react

In separate posts on X, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis blamed the federal Liberals and Prime Minister Mark Carney for failing to do enough to protect workers.

items.title: What we know - and what we don’t - as Nvidia investigates an alleged spy plot involving its CEO
items.description: Stunning allegations of a spy plot have prompted Nvidia to investigate whether its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”

items._ogDesc: Stunning allegations of a spy plot have prompted Nvidia to investigate whether its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”
items.body:
Stunning allegations of a spy plot have prompted Nvidia to investigate whether its founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.”

Huang on Sunday admitted to having an extramarital affair, and acknowledged that news reports surrounding the relationship and potential national security concerns led Nvidia’s board to investigate. He and his chipmaking company did not name the person he had been intimate with, but The New York Times identified her as business executive and Chinese citizen Alice Huang. The outlet said U.S. intelligence determined she was gathering information for Beijing.

China’s Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations on Monday, saying they amount to a smear campaign against Beijing.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Many questions remain unanswered. But the scandal is already bringing turmoil to California-based Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang himself has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on President Donald Trump’s side in Washington.

Here’s what we know.

What Nvidia has said about its investigation

On Sunday, Nvidia announced that its board was initiating an independent investigation. The company cited recent reporting about Huang being “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. The company added that Huang would remain CEO — and that he had committed to cooperating fully during the investigation.

“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”

Jensen Huang apologizes for affair

In a separate email to Nvidia employees, later also published by the company, Huang apologized for his affair.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” Huang wrote, adding that he was “deeply sorry” and that his colleagues also “deserve better” from him.

Huang also reiterated his support for the board’s investigation. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” he said Sunday.

Huang, 63, founded Nvidia more than three decades ago. He and his wife, Lori, reportedly have two children who both work at Nvidia.

China rejects spy allegation claims

China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Nvidia’s CEO.

“The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a routine briefing Monday.

The New York Times reported that Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia. Last year, Megaspeed faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China — which the company in December maintained there was “no evidence” of.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Megaspeed bought more than US$4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times. Last month, the outlet reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia’s Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing.

Huang’s relationship with Washington

Beyond rising to fame in the AI space (often accompanied by his signature leather jacket), Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president’s second term in office. He’s among tech CEOs who have dined at the White House, and even traveled on Air Force One.

Trump has called Huang “smart” and “amazing,” repeatedly insisting he accompany him on foreign trips. After news of Nvidia’s investigation broke, the president said on Sunday the two hadn’t spoken but that he hoped “everything’s fine.”

He continued to praise Huang, including when asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying.

“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He’s done an amazing job for our country,” Trump told reporters. He added that he was still open to taking Huang on his trip to Asia next week.

Questions of wider ramifications for trading AI chips

Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies. And it’s become a leader for making chips that power AI.

Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Trump’s approval for selling its H200 chips in January. Those are not the company’s most cutting-edge chips, but are still powerful. Nvidia has said in regulatory filings that it has sold only a small amount to China, as such sales are also restricted by the Chinese government.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Nvidia’s investigation into whether Huang was a target of foreign intelligence is still ongoing, but some analysts suspect that the allegations will strengthen calls for stricter export controls with China.

“The high-profile nature of these allegations could make it increasingly difficult for Washington to avoid a response,” analysts at Raymond James wrote in a Sunday note.

They said the espionage reports will likely bolster congressional support for legislation aimed at further restricting semiconductor and chipmaking equipment sales to China, which could in turn renew strain over trade between the two countries overall.

Shares of Nvidia sank nearly five per cent as of midday Monday. Stocks for other AI-related companies, including Advanced Micro Devices and Coreweave, meanwhile climbed higher.

Wyatte Grantham-philips, The Associated Press

Shares of Nvidia tumbled more than five per cent Monday after the computer chip maker, central to the artificial intelligence race, opened an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Nvidia’s announcement of the investigation on Sunday followed Huang’s acknowledgment that he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China.

China’s Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations Monday, calling them a smear campaign against Beijing.

Nvidia chips power many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China’s access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology.

There’s a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post, wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., saying that Huang is “not replaceable.”

“On the heels of last week’s Blue Tidal Wave this will also increase momentum for more regulatory scrutiny in the Beltway especially around China and chip restrictions at a time the AI Arms Race is heating up into its next gear between the US and China,” Ives wrote.

Still, Ives said there is a risk, as Huang could be removed as CEO depending on the board’s investigation and that it will remain an overhang on shares near term.

Shares of Nvidia and other major AI companies have sold off steadily since early October, however on growing fears of a bubble in the sector. Nvidia has fallen 23 per cent in the last 30 days, including the sell-off Monday.

The post Canada To Add 200,000 Permanent Resident Spots, Housing Boost Limited appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canada’s Budget 2026 adds 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, but the housing demand boost is limited as recipients already live here.
items.body:
Canada is adjusting its immigration plan after a recent slowdown in population growth. Budget 2026 shows the country is adding 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027. On top of regular admissions and existing programs, the total can exceed 580,000 spots by the end of next year. However, this won’t add much to housing demand, as the extra spaces aim to retain people already here and reduce population churn.

Canadian Immigration Targets Vs Reality

Before diving into the changes, let’s clarify that immigration targets aren’t hard numbers. Ottawa isn’t just making a DoorDash order for 10,000 Guinean students; it sets a target. Meeting that target depends on global demand, domestic processing, and applicant follow-through.

IRCC data shows only 216,600 regular permanent resident admissions in the first 8 months of 2026. That’s just 57% of the target with only a third of the year left, making that a tough goal to hit. Canadian taxpayers actually spent millions to create that post-pandemic study permit surge. Ottawa’s caps only appeared after applications cratered, as qualified demand was exhausted. But don’t let that ruin the narrative of unlimited growth that policymakers want you to believe.

It’s important to understand that immigration targets are similar to a public company’s earnings projections, but instead of boosting a stock price, they bolster Canada’s projected economic growth and access to debt. Whether global demand is there to fulfil the targets remains to be seen. Now let’s move on to the changes.

Canada Trims Temporary Arrivals, Adds 200k Permanent Resident Spots

Budget 2026 reveals fewer new temporary arrivals and more permanent spots. The 2027 immigration targets maintain 380,000 regular permanent admissions and 370,000 new temporary arrivals annually through 2029. That’s a 3.9% reduction (15,000 spots) in new temporary arrivals from the 2026 target, as previously announced. The big change is additional targeted permanent resident spots.

Canada plans to add up to 200,000 permanent resident spots in 2027, up to 100,000 for workers and their families, and up to 100,000 for specified humanitarian and family applicants. Combined with the existing target, it lifts potential permanent resident admissions to 580,000, 52.6% higher than the regular admission target. That’s on top of the earlier initiatives that targeted the transition of 148,000 temporary to permanent residents in 2026-27. Admissions could exceed 580,000 with those earlier initiatives.

Interestingly, it’s accompanied by a reduction to the Federal High Skilled admissions program, which will fall from the previously planned target of 111,000 people to 100,000. However, provincial nominee admissions will rise by 2,500 to 95,000, while the Atlantic Immigration Program rises from 4,000 to 6,000 targeted admissions. Rather than an outright reduction, it looks like Ottawa is hoping to better target regional growth.

More Permanent Residents Don’t Mean More Population Growth

The addition of 200,000 permanent residents won’t directly add to aggregate demand, especially housing. These admissions will only shift people from temporary residents to permanent ones, so their consumption is already reflected today. This distinction was also made clear by the PBO earlier this year, when they reported 48% of permanent residents in 2025 were previously international students or temporary workers.

As we explained earlier this year, Ottawa promised to reduce non-permanent residents as a share of the population, but was initially light on the details. Part of that plan is to turn temporary residents into permanent ones, which the PBO found necessary under the previous plan to hit the target of below 5% by the end of 2027, a delay of a year. Budget 2026 appears to be buying policymakers some more room to help them hit that target.

items._ogDesc: Honda Canada announced Monday it will invest $166 million to upgrade and retool its Alliston, Ont., manufacturing plant, securing more than 4,000 jobs and expanding production of future hybrid-electric vehicles and engines.
items.body:
Honda Canada announced Monday it will invest $166 million to upgrade and retool its Alliston, Ont., manufacturing plant, securing more than 4,000 jobs and expanding production of future hybrid-electric vehicles and engines.

Expanding hybrid-electric vehicle production

The announcement comes just days after Honda celebrated its 40th anniversary and is part of a broader $867 million commitment to bolster its North American manufacturing network and meet growing demand for hybrid vehicles.

Honda Canada President and CEO Dave Jamieson said it reinforces the company’s long-standing commitment to Canadian manufacturing.

“For 40 years, Honda associates in Alliston have demonstrated the skill, innovation and commitment that have made our Canadian operations a cornerstone of Honda’s manufacturing network in North America,” said Jamieson.

He added that the money will help “position the Canadian operations for long-term competitiveness and future opportunities” while benefiting suppliers and the broader economy.

“Honda’s renewed investment in Alliston is a strong vote of confidence in our community, our skilled workforce and the future of automotive manufacturing here in New Tecumseth,” said Mayor-Elect Stephanie MacLellan.

MacLellan said the news is reason for optimism, but noted there is still important work ahead.

“We need to continue working with Honda and our provincial and federal partners to support a competitive automotive sector, protect local jobs and create the conditions for continued investment in our community,” she added.

Honda says it is working with the federal and Ontario governments on the project.

$15B electric vehicle plans shelved in May

This announcement comes on the heels of Honda’s decision in May to indefinitely pause its planned $15 billion EV expansion in Alliston.

The move came shortly after the automaker reported a $2.7 billion full year loss, which it attributed largely to the “high costs of developing electric vehicles” and shifting market conditions as U.S. policy moves away from EV incentives.

Instead, Honda said it would focus more heavily on hybrid vehicles, which continue to see stronger consumer demand than fully electric models.

There has been no further update on the status at this time.

New $3 billion U.S. auto plant in Ohio

The Canadian announcement comes with a major expansion of Honda’s operations in the United States.

Honda also announced Monday that it plans to invest $3 billion in a new automotive manufacturing plant in Ohio, creating more than 2,000 jobs and increasing its U.S. auto production capacity to roughly 1.3 million vehicles annually.

The new Ohio facility will be built between Honda’s existing East Liberty and Marysville assembly plants. It is expected to begin production in 2029, pending final government approvals.

According to Honda, the facility will be able to manufacture nearly 240,000 vehicles annually.

The plant will be designed to produce hybrid-electric, gasoline-powered and battery-electric vehicles, giving greater flexibility to respond to changing market needs.

In May, Honda announced plans to launch 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030, with North America as a key market.

The company says investments in manufacturing facilities across Canada, Ohio, Alabama and Georgia will help support production of these vehicles in North America.

Together, the projects will boost Honda’s U.S. production capacity to nearly 1.3 million vehicles annually and raise its North American capacity to roughly 1.9 million, according to the automaker.

items.title: Here are the 7 luxury markets outperforming Toronto and Vancouver
items.description: REMAX Canada finds five markets posting double-digit gains as larger urban centres pull back
items.content: <p>REMAX Canada finds five markets posting double-digit gains as larger urban centres pull back</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_638175884653377179.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: REMAX Canada finds five markets posting double-digit gains as larger urban centres pull back
items.body:
Seven of 13 Canadian luxury housing markets recorded year-over-year sales increases in the nine months to September 30, with five posting double-digit gains, even as Greater Vancouver and the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) retreated sharply, according to REMAX Canada’s Fall/Winter 2026 Spotlight on Luxury Report.

Burlington led national luxury growth at 26.3%, followed by St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador (+21%), Calgary (+20.6%), Edmonton (+15.9%), and Saskatoon (+15.3%).

Ottawa (+7.6%) and Winnipeg (+3%) also posted gains.

Greater Vancouver fell 17%, Oakville 16.7%, and the GTA 9.4% at their respective luxury thresholds, a divergence the publication has tracked since Canada’s sharpest housing market split in years became visible in first-quarter data.

Don Kottick, President of REMAX Canada, said conventional market variables are no longer the whole story.

“Regional economic strength is shaping luxury demand, with stronger economies providing a sturdier foundation for homebuying activity,” Kottick said.

“Traditional drivers such as supply and demand, pricing, purchasing power and interest rates alone are no longer the only reliable predictors of market activity. Market dynamics are evolving, becoming more complex and nuanced, and increasingly dependent on regional fundamentals.”

What’s driving gains in smaller markets

The theme is consistent with what CMP reported in June, when tracking why luxury buyers are leaving major markets for smaller cities had shifted from a cyclical question to a structural one.

“Smaller and mid-sized markets are experiencing increasing or stable conditions at the higher end of the luxury segment, largely supported by economic diversification, population growth, and continued demand for lifestyle-oriented properties,” Kottick told CMP at the time.

“Meanwhile, in the country’s largest and more expensive markets, uncertainty has prompted affluent buyers to take a more measured approach.”

Ultra-luxury holds above the declines

Despite headline drops in Toronto and Vancouver, the top of the market proved more durable.

GTA sales above $7.5 million climbed 17.6% year over year, with 15 transactions exceeding $10 million in the City of Toronto, the highest tally in a decade.

Oakville sales above $5 million rose close to 18%, even as overall luxury sales above $3.25 million fell 16.7%.

Greater Vancouver’s detached market above $5 million declined 8%, significantly less than the 17% drop in the broader segment above $3 million.

A development since the study period closed also bears watching: the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, adding a fresh financing variable for buyers dependent on mortgages or the sale of an existing home.

Michael Altneu, Vice President of Luxury at REMAX Canada, said buyer readiness is not in question. Confidence is.

“Wealth enables a home purchase; confidence and the right opportunity motivate it,” Altneu said.

“Most luxury buyers have the financial resources to act, but economic and geopolitical concerns are giving purchasers reason to pause. That said, a property that meets their every expectation can still spur a buyer, especially given the narrower price gap between existing homes and move-up properties, particularly in smaller markets.”

That narrowing gap, a pattern consistent with how secondary luxury markets are outshining Toronto and Vancouver in sales velocity, also drove some of the report’s most notable transactions: a $28-million waterfront estate in Vancouver, a Forest Hill home in Toronto that sold for more than $23 million, and an $18.5-million waterfront property in Oakville.

items.description: Canada’s largest bank eyes Asia-Pacific growth with Melbourne-based fund manager deal
items.content: <p>Canada’s largest bank eyes Asia-Pacific growth with Melbourne-based fund manager deal</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639298482233952768.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s largest bank eyes Asia-Pacific growth with Melbourne-based fund manager deal
items.body:
Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) has agreed to acquire Yarra Capital Management Limited, an independent Australian fund manager overseeing approximately A$18 billion in assets as at September 30.

The deal places Canada’s largest bank firmly on the Asia-Pacific map and signals an increasingly global strategy for one of the country’s most dominant financial institutions.

The agreement is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending satisfaction of certain conditions including regulatory approval from Australian authorities.

RBC confirmed the transaction will not significantly affect its common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio — the standard measure of a bank’s financial buffer under international banking rules — or its future run-rate earnings.

Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

A springboard for global asset management

Founded in 1864 and listed on both the Toronto Stock Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange, Royal Bank of Canada is Canada’s largest bank by market capitalisation.

Its asset management arm, RBC Global Asset Management (RBC GAM), oversaw approximately $1.70 trillion in assets as at July 31, with the bank’s wealth management segment delivering total revenue of CA$6.41 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2026, up 16% year over year.

RBC GAM is a provider of global investment management services and solutions to institutional, high-net-worth and individual investors through separate accounts, pooled funds, mutual funds, hedge funds, exchange-traded funds and specialty investment strategies.

The acquisition follows earlier international moves by RBC GAM, including the purchase of London-based fixed income specialist BlueBay Asset Management, and extends a deliberate push to build market share outside North America. 

"The investment and distribution capabilities of Yarra are complementary to our asset management business. Yarra’s reputation within Australian fixed income and equities is a testament to its strong track record in investment performance and culture of putting clients first," said Damon Williams, chief executive officer of RBC GAM in Toronto.

 "We know Australian institutional investors and intermediaries take a globally oriented approach to asset allocation. We believe the strength of our investment capabilities that go beyond domestic borders within fixed income, equities and alternatives are well-positioned to support this investor appetite."

An independent Australian firm with Asia-Pacific reach

Founded in 2017, Yarra Capital Management operates from offices in Melbourne and Sydney.

The firm specialises in Australian fixed income, equities, and alternative investment solutions, with access to international equity strategies through third-party manager partnerships.

Yarra serves the Australian institutional and retail markets, and its Australian investment products are accessed from various international markets, including Japan and New Zealand. 

Dion Hershan, executive chairman of Yarra Capital Management in Melbourne, described the agreement as the result of a thorough and deliberate search:

“After a long and deliberate search to find the right business partner for the future, we are thrilled about our agreement to join RBC. The strong cultural alignment between Yarra and RBC is very clear and we share the same fundamental beliefs of serving our clients with compelling products and services, delivering investment excellence and developing and retaining the best talent.”

For Canadian mortgage professionals tracking where the Big Six are directing capital, the acquisition points unmistakably outward.

Marcos De Souza, a banking analyst at Morningstar DBRS in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in December 2025 that domestic consolidation options were fast narrowing.

“The Canadian market is so small,” De Souza said. “There’s not much further merger and acquisition space in 2026 in the Canadian sense. I don’t know where it would come from.”

With the Yarra deal, RBC has found its answer across the Pacific.

items.title: FSRA issues conditions on Ontario agent over unpaid 2018 penalty
items.description: Agent settles with FSRA, agreeing to pay a $30,000 penalty outstanding since 2018
items.content: <p>Agent settles with FSRA, agreeing to pay a $30,000 penalty outstanding since 2018</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639298474539637558.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Agent settles with FSRA, agreeing to pay a $30,000 penalty outstanding since 2018
items.body:
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) has imposed conditions on the insurance agent licence of Victor Ferreira following a settlement over administrative penalties that went unpaid for more than six years.

Ferreira and his company, Ferreira Insurance and Investment Concepts Inc. (FIIC), failed to pay administrative monetary penalties (AMPs) of $30,000 and $45,000 respectively, both imposed in April 2018 for conduct contrary to the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 (MBLAA).

Despite invoices issued by the Ontario Minister of Finance in September 2019, neither sum was paid.

FIIC has since withdrawn its insurance agent licence renewal application.

A decade of deferred consequences

Ferreira had also held a mortgage agent licence under the MBLAA from August 25, 2015, until its expiry on March 31, 2018.

Ontario’s former financial regulator, the Financial Services Commission of Ontario (FSCO), identified conduct contrary to the MBLAA between 2013 and 2015.

A 2018 settlement with FSCO produced the AMPs, neither of which was paid even after the Minister of Finance issued invoices in September 2019.

The case grew more complex when it emerged that across three successive renewal applications – filed in 2018, 2021, and 2023 – both Ferreira and FIIC answered “No” to questions about past regulatory discipline.

FSRA issued a Notice of Proposal in May 2024 to refuse both applications on grounds of unsuitability, citing the unpaid penalties and those misstatements.

False statements on licence applications have become a recurring element in recent FSRA enforcement files.

A settlement reached December 20, 2024 resolved the matter without a Financial Services Tribunal hearing.

Ferreira agreed to pay the $30,000 AMP, and FIIC withdrew its renewal application.

His insurance agent licence was renewed under two-year conditions: mandatory supervision by a licenced insurance agent with at least two years of experience, a bar on supervising other agents, a prohibition on holding significant control over any licenced insurance corporation, and quarterly written reports to FSRA’s senior manager.

The order was issued January 10, 2025.

A Laval man has been convicted on eight fraud counts after secretly registering high-interest mortgages on properties he had agreed to purchase, leaving homeowners unable to recover what they were owed. https://t.co/B1yeEAer5s — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 5, 2026

Part of a broader enforcement wave

The case arrives as FSRA’s enforcement actions surged across all regulated sectors in 2024–25, with the regulator initiating 100 actions, up from 65 the year prior, and imposing approximately $1.2 million in AMPs – the majority in mortgage brokering.

Elissa Sinha, director of litigation and enforcement at FSRA, wrote in the regulator’s first annual enforcement report that “enforcement is critical to FSRA’s mandate to protect consumers, promote high business standards, and deter fraud and misconduct in regulated sectors.”

Established brokers have welcomed the shift. “I’ve seen more cases against bad actors in the last 12 to 18 months than in previous years,” Joe Sammut, broker of record at Mortgage Architects – A Better Way in Ontario, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in a March interview on FSRA’s tougher enforcement stance.

“They seem to be clamping down and cleaning up, and they’re making sure the fines they’re enacting on people are publicized. They’re finally taking seriously the role we play as mortgage professionals in the transaction. It’s frustrating to see the lack of professionalism [from some mortgage agents]. But I think what the latest regulation is doing is making the good ones even better and the bad ones are that much more obvious.”

Carmen Costa, principal broker at TCG Lending Centres in Ontario, shared a similar view, saying Ontario’s framework is “appropriate, and in many ways necessary” because “strong oversight is important” when dealing with complex financial products that can reshape clients’ finances.

items.title: Westbank’s West End vision hits a wall in BC Supreme Court
items.description: The developer’s second receivership in months raises hard questions about Vancouver’s condo future
items.content: <p>The developer’s second receivership in months raises hard questions about Vancouver’s condo future</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639298455212005902.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The developer’s second receivership in months raises hard questions about Vancouver’s condo future
items.body:
A BC Supreme Court judge has placed a stalled West End condo development under receivership – the second Westbank Holdings Ltd. project to face such action in 2026.

Justice Kevin D. Loo appointed MNP Ltd. as receiver on November 4, after a credit agreement dating to 2016 collapsed under the weight of mounting unpaid debt owed to Bank of Montreal (BMO).

The proceeding, docketed as Bank of Montreal v 700 Bidwell Holdings Inc. (2026 BCSC 2149), names 700 Bidwell Holdings Inc., 700 Bidwell Limited Partnership, 700 Bidwell Property Inc., and Westbank Holdings Ltd.

It follows the April 2026 receivership of Joyce 2, a separate Westbank project.

A decade in the making

The site at 1668 and 1684 Alberni Street in Vancouver’s West End has been in development since August 2017, when a rezoning application was filed for a proposed 40-storey tower containing 128 strata units.

Vancouver City Council approved the rezoning in May 2022, but a development permit application was cancelled in September 2025, the same period in which interest payments under the BMO credit agreement ceased.

Justice Loo set out the financial damage in blunt terms in his written reasons.

“The respondents owe the bank more than $36 million. The respondents have failed to make interest payments when due since at least September 2025, and they have failed to repay the outstanding debt following a demand on January 26, 2026. Since issuance of that demand, the bank debt has increased by over $914,850 in accrued interest, plus costs.”

“At the end of the day, it is clear in this case that the debt is not being paid,” Loo concluded.

The respondents conceded they had made no proposals to repay what was owed, despite earlier promises to do so, and acknowledged the bank had extended repeated opportunities to resolve the defaults, none of which were acted upon.

Interest was accruing at approximately $5,150 per day, with more than $300,000 accumulating since the petition was filed on August 12, 2026. Rental income collected from tenants in the existing buildings had also not been remitted to BMO as required under the agreement.

Loo also flagged the complexity of any potential sale.

“I can infer, despite the paltry evidence in this regard, that any transaction with respect to the lands will not be simple.”

Receiverships rising as Vancouver’s condo market stalls

The ruling arrives as real estate receiverships surge nationally. Lauren White, executive vice-president of CBRE’s land services group in Toronto, identified the structural cause: “These projects that are under construction, they’ve seen such a rise in prices that they just, they run out of money.”

Investor activity in Metro Vancouver’s pre-construction market collapsed from roughly 50% of buyers between 2020 and 2023 to just 7% by 2025, according to Rennie Intelligence data.

“Right now, the market is out of gas,” Ryan Berlin, head economist and vice-president at Rennie Intelligence in Vancouver, previously said.

“Nothing is working for developers. It’s not really working for buyers. So, we’re just kind of stagnating right now.”

Justice Loo gave the respondents until February 13, 2027, to refinance before MNP Ltd. can proceed with any sale.

Westbank says it will appeal. “There is no basis for this filing and we will be submitting an appeal,” the company told CTV News.

“We have no further comment.”

items._ogDesc: Move to extend but adjust foreign buyer ban was the right call, says Ownright co-founder and COO
items.body:
Canada’s federal government is keeping the foreign homebuyer ban in place but adjusting it to exclude newly built properties – a move that could provide a real boost new construction if executed well, according to a prominent mortgage industry executive.

Joel Fox (pictured top), co-founder and chief operating officer at digital real estate law platform Ownright, told Canadian Mortgage Professional he viewed the announcement as the most potentially significant measure for housing in the near term contained in last week’s Budget.

He said the original blanket ban had inadvertently deprived the preconstruction sector of a key source of demand: foreign investment, which has traditionally played an important role in stoking new homebuilding.

“We talk constantly about how there’s not enough homes in the country and the housing shortage,” Fox said. “And then in the same vein, we’ve had this restriction on foreign homeownership, which was actually very much floating the new build space for a long period of time.”

Non-resident foreign buyers will still be forbidden from accessing Canada’s resale market, a decision described by Fox as a sensible one that will likely boost supply while avoiding the reemergence of concerns around speculative purchasing.

There’s still a risk, though, with the move: namely, that outside buyers might simply purchase units and leave them vacant, a trend that drew significant criticism before the ban was introduced and factored among the Trudeau government’s main reasons for first implementing it in early 2023.

“What we can’t afford, or what we don’t want to have happen, is that those places just sit empty,” Fox said. “Ideally those are occupied by either the owners or made available for rent.”

Feds prioritize long-term thinking rather than short-term solutions

The budget also included a reported $45 billion commitment to housing measures over the next decade, a pledge that Fox said was significant even if it offers little immediate relief to buyers and industry professionals hoping for a swift bounce-back in market activity.

“There’s no doubt that this budget is built to make long-term impacts n the housing market, and it certainly falls short of making a near-term impact,” he said. “In a lot of ways, I actually think that’s the right approach.”

Measures to improve housing affordability in the short term have been a staple of previous governments, but many have proven fruitless or ultimately been scrapped.

Among the most noteworthy of those was the First-Time Home Buyer Incentive, a shared-equity scheme operated between 2019 and 2024 that mortgage industry members said had little uptake – particularly in pricier markets.

Fox said previous governments had been “guilty of making short-term corrections that don’t necessarily net out over the long term” and that the current budget reflected a better philosophy, one that accepts the housing crisis won’t be solved quickly.

“The resolution to our housing issues isn’t going to come from short-term measures that temporarily move the needle,” he said. “It’s a long-term belief that we need more housing.”

Trade war takes government's main focus away from housing

While the foreign homebuyer ban extension and adjustment drew headlines, housing was far from the main focus of the budget – particularly with the US-Canada trade war rumbling on and the federal government still taking steps to deepen Canadian trading relationships away from the US.

Strengthening the economic outlook and in turn building up consumer confidence are important, Fox noted, more so than potential measures to help more Canadians into homes in the immediate future.

“Whatever those short-term measures might be addressing isn’t really addressing the bigger picture, which is the broader economic uncertainty that’s being driven by south of the border,” he said.

Prime minister Mark Carney’s efforts to diversify Canada’s trade dependence beyond the US are, in Fox’s view, a strategy that will pay off over time, even if the impact isn’t immediately apparent.

“A lot of the stuff that Carney and his government are doing to build trade relationships with countries outside of the US – I believe that’s going to compound over time to build confidence back up,” he said. “But again, it’s all a long game.”

items.title: Insider: Budget 2026 Opens Up Financing For Small Rental Builders
items.description:
A developer who shelved a small rental project over financing has a reason to price it again.

Budget 2026 gives newly built triplexes and fourplexes access to insured loans of up to 90% of completed value. It also lets private insurers cover buildings with five to 50 units.

Budget 2026, tabled November 5, pairs those changes with more money for Build Canada Homes. For a smaller builder, the mortgage rules are the part to take to a lender first: how much cash would the project need up front, and could the finished building support the loan?

Keep the rent assumptions where they were for that comparison. Otherwise, it becomes hard to tell whether the financing has improved the project or the spreadsheet has simply become more optimistic.

Different rules on either side of five units

The Department of Finance's technical rules take effect for insurance applications lenders submit on or after February 1, 2027. The unit count determines which rules apply.

For buildings with five to 50 units, term financing requires a minimum debt coverage ratio of 1.15 for a five-year term or 1.10 for a ten-year term. Borrowers need net worth equal to at least 25% of the requested loan, with a $100,000 minimum, based on Canadian assets. Separately titled properties cannot be bundled to meet the unit requirement.

Construction loans are assessed separately. Insurers set their own debt-servicing criteria during construction; the prescribed amortization and debt coverage requirements apply to term financing. Borrowers using the new three- and four-unit option also have to pass personal qualification tests for the long-term mortgage.

A fourplex and a six-unit building can face quite different borrowing limits on the same site. The six-unit design may qualify for a longer amortization, but it may also cost more to build. Compare the extra debt with the extra cost and rent before choosing the larger project.

Compare the new loans with CMHC

CMHC Standard Rental Housing already covers eligible properties with at least five units. It allows borrowing of up to 85% of value, with amortizations of up to 50 years for new construction and 40 years for existing properties.

MLI Select offers different terms in exchange for commitments to affordability, energy efficiency or accessibility. Eligible new construction can qualify for up to 95% loan-to-cost, depending on the points earned and the program's other requirements.

The new private-insurer rules add another option to that comparison. Be careful with the percentages: 90% of appraised value and 95% of project cost can produce quite different loan amounts.

Ask for offers that cover the same project and construction schedule. Compare the interest rate and insurance premium, then work through guarantees, reserve requirements and conditions on each draw. A larger approved loan can be less useful if its costs are higher or the money arrives too late to pay the contractor.

The rent limits the loan

Take a hypothetical new rental building worth $5 million, with annual net operating income of $225,000. At a 5% mortgage rate, a 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage, the income supports about $3.62 million of debt. A loan at 90% of the building's value would be $4.5 million.

That leaves a gap of roughly $881,000 between the advertised maximum and what the income can support.

Illustrative calculation: a $4.5-million value ceiling versus income-based capacity of about $4.25 million at 4%, $3.62 million at 5% and $3.13 million at 6%. Assumes 50-year amortization and 1.15 debt coverage.

These calculations apply to the mortgage after construction. They use monthly payments and Canadian nominal rates compounded semi-annually, and exclude insurance premiums, fees and reserves. The rates are examples rather than lender quotes. An insurer may also use different income and expense assumptions when it assesses the property.

A builder can tie up less equity and still be taking on more risk. The loan has to be serviced through vacancies, repairs and a slower-than-expected lease-up. Those expenses belong in the operating budget before anyone calculates how much debt the building can carry.

Get the construction loan and the permanent mortgage assessed together. If the finished property cannot support enough mortgage debt to repay the construction lender, the builder has to find the difference.

Build Canada Homes funding starts later

The budget proposes another $13 billion in cash capital for Build Canada Homes over ten years, beginning in 2028–29. That would bring its capitalization to $45 billion. Ottawa's target is 200,000 homes over the next decade; delivery will depend on projects moving through approvals and construction.

It also proposes $1.5 billion over four years from 2027–28 for infrastructure on federal land, plus $387.4 million in later years. A builder considering a partnership needs to know when a particular site will be serviced and when the money will be available. Procurement terms will determine who can take part.

Source: Department of Finance missing-middle backgrounder and Budget 2026 Chapter 3, November 5, 2026. Fiscal-year funding starts are not home-completion dates.

Public land and long-term capital can help build housing for people whose rents cannot cover the cost of new construction. The operating budget needs funding, too. Taxes, maintenance and repairs continue long after the building opens.

For market rental projects, the effect will depend partly on the supply of buildable sites. Easier financing can help developers start viable projects. Where land and approvals are scarce, buyers may instead use the extra borrowing room to bid more for the same sites.

Reprice the project before bidding more for land

Run the available financing options against the same operating budget. Then confirm which lenders and insurers will offer them, what they need to approve an application and how the construction loan converts to a term mortgage. February 1 is the start date for lender submissions, so allow time for approval and funding.

For a small developer, the useful result is a loan commitment that makes a viable project possible.

If the numbers work only after raising the projected rents or cutting the repair allowance, the financing problem is still there.
